summary: Gives terminology and a model of a typical Network Access Server (NAS), the device that connects dial-up users to a network. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: A Network Access Server is the device a dial-up or tunneled user meets first on their way into a network. RFC 2881 sets out a model of what that device is, what it does, and what it needs from the servers that hold user accounts, so that protocols such as RADIUS can be evaluated against a common picture.

questions: what is a network access server
how does a nas authenticate users
how does a nas do accounting
subtitle: A reference picture of the device that lets a dial-up or tunneled user into a network

tldr.problem: The Network Access Server is the first device most users meet on their way into a network, and the idea had grown up over the years without ever being formally defined or analysed.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes a reference model of a NAS: client interfaces where users arrive, a network interface to the networks they are granted access to, a policy management interface for per-user service, and a device management interface for the operator. Authentication, authorization, accounting and auditing are separated out and delegated to an AAAA server.
tldr.outcome: The model gives protocol designers a common reference to evaluate NAS service protocols against, such as RADIUS and Diameter, and it lists the security concerns a NAS has to handle. The memo describes a model rather than a particular solution.

facts.label: Typical RAM in a NAS
facts.value: 1MB to 8MB, varying with the number of ports

facts.label: Client interface classes
facts.value: 2: dial access servers and tunnel servers

today: RFC 2881 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes a model rather than a particular product, so it is read today as a shared vocabulary for the parts of a network access server and the jobs it delegates to an AAAA server.

sections.title: The First Device a User Meets
sections.content:
A Network Access Server is the initial entry point to a network for most users of network services. It is the first device in the network to provide services to an end user, and it acts as a gateway for all further services. Its importance to users and providers alike is paramount. The concept, however, grew up over the years without ever being formally defined or analysed.

This memo therefore describes a model for evaluating NAS service protocols such as RADIUS and the Diameter work. It gives examples of typical NAS hardware and software features, but says plainly that these are illustrative rather than hard limits, and that an important goal is a framework that allows further development and expansion of capabilities in NAS implementations. As with most IETF projects, the focus is on standardising the protocol interaction between the components, so two areas are left out: the back-end implementation of the AAA server is abstracted and not prescribed, leaving the organisation of data, internal interfaces and capabilities to the implementation, and the front-end call technology is not assumed to be static, so that new technologies and services can be added with minimal impact on existing implementations.

The memo also sets out its assumptions about the equipment. A typical hardware-based NAS runs in a constrained system, so the protocols must not assume unlimited resources: a computer system of minimal to moderate performance, with example processors of the Intel 386 or 486 or the Motorola 68000; a moderate but not large amount of RAM, typically 1MB to 8MB depending on the number of ports supported; some small amount of non-volatile memory or a way to be configured out-of-band; and no assumption of a local file system or disk storage. A NAS may be a system of interconnected specialised processor units, typically circuit boards arrayed in a card cage and referred to by their slot number.
sections.plainLanguage: Most people meet the network through a device that checks who they are and lets them in: a dial-up server or the far end of a tunnel. This memo draws a picture of that device, so that the protocols used between it and the servers that hold user accounts can be judged against a common idea of what it has to do.

sections.title: The Reference Model of a NAS
sections.content:
The memo gives a diagram of a NAS, its dependencies and its interfaces, and says it is an abstraction meant as a reference rather than a picture of any particular implementation. Users arrive at the top, over modems on the public telephone network or through encapsulated connections. Below that sits the NAS itself, with a client interface where end users request access, routing, and a network interface that connects to the networks access is being granted to.

The client interfaces come in two broad classes, and a single device may serve both. A dial access server has client interfaces that are modems, local or remote, attached to the public telephone network. A tunnel server has client interfaces that are tunnelling endpoints in a protocol such as L2TP. With tunnelling protocols such as L2F, ATMP and L2TP, tunnel server systems have to behave as a virtual NAS, where the calls arrive as tunnelled sessions rather than on hardware ports.

Two management interfaces sit alongside. The policy management interface allows access to network services to be managed on a per-user basis, and may be a configuration file, a graphical user interface, an API, or a protocol such as RADIUS, Diameter or COPS; it provides a mechanism for granular resource management and policy enforcement. The device management interface is how the entity that owns and operates the NAS manages it, and may equally be a configuration file, a graphical user interface, an API, or a protocol such as SNMP. The memo is careful to say the AAA server does not provide network management for the NAS; its purpose is to authorise and characterise the individual services for users, so any feature that can be user specific is open to supply from it.
sections.plainLanguage: The reference picture has users arriving over phone lines or tunnels, a set of client interfaces where they ask for access, routing, and network interfaces to the networks they are being let into. On the side are two management interfaces: one that decides what each user is allowed, and one that lets the operator look after the device itself.

sections.title: The AAAA Functions
sections.content:
The memo then names the pieces of that model. Authentication is the confirmation that a user asking for services is a valid user of those network services, done by presenting an identity and credentials, with passwords, one-time tokens, digital certificates and phone numbers given as examples. Authorization is the granting of specific types of service, including no service at all, based on the authentication, what is being requested and the current system state; it may depend on restrictions such as time of day, physical location, or a ban on multiple logins by the same user. Its examples of service include IP address filtering, address assignment, route assignment, QoS and differential services, bandwidth control, compulsory tunnelling to a specific endpoint, and encryption.

Accounting is the tracking of the consumption of NAS resources by users, for management, planning, billing or other purposes. Real-time accounting is delivered concurrently with the consumption; batch accounting is saved and delivered later. Typical information gathered includes the identity of the user, the nature of the service delivered, when the service began and when it ended. Auditing has a different purpose: instead of tracking consumption, it determines the nature of a user's network activity, such as which hosts were accessed when and which protocols were used.

An AAAA server is a server, or servers, that provide authentication, authorization, accounting and auditing services. The four functions may sit on one server or be broken up among several, and the servers may be co-located with the NAS or, more typically, live on a separate machine and talk to it over an AAAA protocol. Device monitoring is the tracking of the status, activity and usage of the NAS as a network device, and device provisioning is its configurations, settings and control.
sections.plainLanguage: Four jobs are separated out. Authentication checks that the caller really is a valid user. Authorization decides what they may do, including doing nothing at all. Accounting measures what they used, either as it happens or later in a batch. Auditing records what they actually did, such as which hosts they reached and with which protocols. One or more AAAA servers do this work, usually away from the NAS itself.

sections.title: What Happens When a Call Arrives
sections.content:
The typical sequence starts with a call arriving on a port or over the network. On a port, the NAS may auto-detect the type of call. For CLI or SLIP it prompts for a username and password if security is set; for PPP it engages the Link Control Protocol and then authentication. It then asks the AAA server to authenticate the caller and, if the answer is okay, proceeds to service, possibly issuing a challenge and possibly asking for a password change. Over the network, it activates an internal protocol server such as telnet or ftp, engages that protocol's own authentication technique, and confirms the authentication information with the AAA server.

Other kinds of call are described too. Call management services use information from the telephone system or a gateway controller, typically the called or calling number, to decide whether to answer the call or return a busy to the caller, and the server may also need to allocate a port and route the call. Dial-out is triggered when a packet destination matches an outbound route configured in advance, after which profile information is found to set up the call and the AAA server is asked for call details. For VPN and tunnelling, the authentication server identifies the user as remote, the tunnel protocol is invoked to a remote server, authentication information may be forwarded to a remote AAA server, and if it succeeds the local link is given a remote identity. Multi-link aggregation searches for other bundles with the same identifying information, across multiple systems, and joins calls that match on authentication and originator identities into one addressable source with a single IP address. Hardwired services are permanent wide-area connections such as frame relay or permanent virtual circuits, and permanent serial connections such as printers.

Some details of sessions matter to a protocol designer. A session must have a user identifier and an authenticator to complete the authentication process. Accounting starts at the time of the call or service, though finer detail is allowed, and at the end of service the call may be disconnected or allowed to re-authenticate for additional services. Authorization to run services is supplied and applied after authentication, and a NAS may abort the call if the session authorization information disagrees with the characteristics of the call. Accounting messages are sent when service begins and ends, and possibly periodically during it; accounting is not necessarily a real-time service, because the NAS may queue and batch send event records. Only the NAS knows the true dynamic state of a session, so real-time monitoring of port and user status has to come from it.
sections.plainLanguage: A call arrives on a port or over the network. The device works out what kind it is, asks the caller for a name and password or starts the PPP handshake, and asks the AAA server whether the caller is allowed in. If it is, the session starts and the device records what happens so it can be billed. The same shape covers tunneled calls, calls the device makes itself, and groups of calls joined into one connection.

sections.title: Identifying the Caller and Authorizing the Session
sections.content:
A NAS typically supports several authentication systems. For asynchronous terminal users it may be as simple as a prompt and typed input. For network datalink users such as PPP there are several methods, of which PAP, CHAP and MS-CHAP are named, and some of these are themselves protocols, such as EAP and Kerberos. The content of the exchange may not be straightforward either: hard token cards such as the Safeword and SecurID systems generate one-time passphrases that have to be validated against a proprietary server, and where multi-link support exists a session token or certificate may have to be remembered so that later links can be authenticated. In the case of VPN and compulsory tunnelling services, a Network Access Identifier is normally presented by the user; this NAI is parsed into a destination network identifier either by the NAS or by the AAA server, and the authentication information is typically not validated locally but by an AAA service at the remote end of the tunnel.

Once a user has been authenticated, the network management may want to configure and authorise a number of individual pieces of information for that user or class of user. For asynchronous terminal users these include banners, custom prompts, menus and command line macros, which could be shortcuts, compound commands or restrictive scripts. For network users they include addresses and routes, callback instructions, packet and activity filters, and network and host server addresses.

Some services need resources allocated dynamically, and the information about them may not be known during the authentication phase but come up later, for example the IP addresses for multi-link bundles, and the authorization may change over the time of the session. That requires a division of responsibility between the NAS and the AAA server, or cooperation through a stateful service. The services listed are IP address management, concurrent login limitations, tunnel usage limitations, real-time account expirations and call management policies. Where a certain level of service is required and is not available, the request may have to be refused or corrective action taken.

The NAS also interacts with the routing of the IP network it sits in, and these interactions may be controlled on a per-user or per-session basis. Some input streams may be directed to specific hosts other than the default gateway for the destination subnet, and some types of packet may be discarded before entering the network, with filters based on the destination address and port number. Anti-spoofing controls may stop traffic sourced from addresses other than the one assigned to the port. A NAS may also be an edge router that applies quality of service policies, which makes it a policy enforcement point, and it may learn those policies for the user through the AAA service.
sections.plainLanguage: How the caller proves who they are depends on the kind of connection: a typed password for a terminal, one of several challenge methods for PPP, a one-time code from a token card, or a name that says which tunnel to use. Once the caller is known, the provider can hand out per-user settings such as addresses, filters, menus and script-like commands. Some of those settings need resources that are only known later, which is why the provider and the AAA server have to keep working together during the session.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it describes a model rather than a particular solution, and then lists the security concerns a NAS has to take seriously: providing authentication techniques robust enough for the network's policies; letting the NAS authenticate the authentication servers it is configured with; letting the server authenticate the clients it is configured with; hiding authentication information from network snoopers, to protect against attacks and to preserve user privacy; protecting the integrity of message exchanges against attacks such as replay or man-in-the-middle; stopping other hosts from interfering with services authorised to the NAS or gaining unauthorised services; stopping other hosts from probing or guessing at authentication information; protecting the NAS configuration and administration from unauthorised users; and protecting the network from illegal packets sourced by accessing connections.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo closes with a list of what a NAS must protect: strong enough ways of checking callers, checking its own servers and having them check it, keeping passwords out of sight of anyone listening on the network, stopping packets being replayed or altered in flight, stopping other machines on the network from guessing credentials or grabbing services they were not given, keeping the device's own configuration safe, and blocking illegal packets from the people who connect.

viz.caption: THE PARTS OF THE REFERENCE MODEL

items.title: Client interface
items.text: Where end users ask for network access, over modems on the telephone network or over tunnels.

items.title: Routing
items.text: Usually present when the network being reached is a routed network.

items.title: Network interface
items.text: Connects to the networks that access is being granted to.

items.title: Policy management interface
items.text: Manages access per user, through a file, an interface, an API or a protocol such as RADIUS.

items.title: Device management interface
items.text: How the owner of the NAS operates and manages it, for example with SNMP.

items.title: The network or networks
items.text: The networks the NAS is granting access to.

viz.caption: THE CALL ARRIVAL SEQUENCE THE MEMO DESCRIBES

messages.label: CALL ARRIVAL
messages.note: On a port or over the network.

messages.label: AUTHENTICATION REQUEST
messages.note: The NAS asks the AAA server to check the caller.

messages.label: AUTHORIZATION DETAILS
messages.note: What the user is allowed to do and how to record it.

messages.label: SERVICE
messages.note: The session runs, and accounting records are sent at the start and the end.

viz.caption: THE FOUR FUNCTIONS THE MODEL SEPARATES OUT

cells: Confirms that the requester is a valid user of the network services requested
Passwords, one-time tokens, digital certificates, phone numbers
Grants specific types of service, including no service at all
IP address filtering, address assignment, bandwidth control, compulsory tunnelling, encryption
Tracks the consumption of NAS resources by users
User identity, nature of the service, when it began and when it ended
Determines the nature of a user's network activity rather than their consumption
Which hosts were accessed when, and which protocols were used
